title: Where are you from?
goal: Say where you come from and where you live, say which languages you speak, and set up the rule that drives the rest of this course: a noun's gender can be guessed from its last letter.
bekal: answer *Odkiaľ si?* and *Kde bývaš?* with the right forms
guess the gender of any noun from its last letter — right more than nine times out of ten
negate any verb with the joined prefix *ne-*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — V kaviarni po hodine
dialogs.intro: After class, Eva and Budi sit in the café across from the school. Eva wants to know more.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: Ja som z Košíc, ale teraz bývam v Bratislave.
lines.id: I'm from Košice, but now I live in Bratislava.
lines.literal: I I-am from Košice, but now I-live in Bratislava.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ja tu bývam len dva mesiace.
lines.id: I've only lived here for two months.
lines.literal: I here I-live only two months.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: A little. I don't speak well yet.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.id: Never mind. What languages do you speak?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Po indonézsky, po anglicky a trochu po nemecky.
lines.id: Indonesian, English, and a little German.
lines.literal: in-the-way Indonesian, in-the-way English and a-little in-the-way German.

lines.speaker: Eva:
lines.text: To je super! Ja neviem po nemecky.
lines.id: That's great! I don't speak German.
lines.literal: that is super! I not-I-know in-the-way German.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ale vieš po slovensky. To je ťažší jazyk.
lines.id: But you speak Slovak. That's a harder language.
lines.literal: but you-know in-the-way Slovak. that is harder language.

notes: **Z + place name = "from".** It forces a special form that is set out fully in unit 9: *Indonézia → z Indonézie*, *Košice → z Košíc*, *Slovensko → zo Slovenska*. For now learn the ready-made forms; the pattern will become clear on its own later.

**Z becomes zo before words starting with s or z.** *zo Slovenska*, *zo Zvolena*. Slovak does this with several short prepositions: *v/vo*, *s/so*, *k/ku*, *z/zo*. The reason is purely physical — two hissing sounds in a row are hard to say.

**Nehovorím, neviem, nevadí — the prefix ne- joins on.** This is the general rule for every verb except *byť*. Notice that the stress moves to the prefix: *HOH-voh-reem* becomes *NEH-hoh-voh-reem*. The prefix *ne-* becomes the first syllable, and the first syllable is always stressed.
**Nevadí is a complete sentence.** Literally "it doesn't bother" — used exactly like "never mind" and "no problem". You'll hear it dozens of times a day in Slovakia.

**Vedieť is not poznať.** *Vieš po slovensky* = you **can speak** Slovak (a skill). For "to know someone" Slovak uses *poznať*: *Poznám Evu*. The difference is the same as French *savoir* and *connaître*, and it is set out fully in unit 16.

grammars.title: Noun gender — twenty seconds that decide the rest of this course
body: Every Slovak noun has one of three genders, and that gender decides which case endings it takes. The good news: you can almost always guess it from **the last letter of the basic form**, without memorizing anything.
after: **The last two rows are the only ones that need attention.** A word ending in a consonant is usually masculine, unless that consonant is a soft *ď, ť, ň, ľ* or the ending *-osť* — then it's feminine. Learn that exception and your accuracy rises to about ninety percent.

**One exception that makes sense: people.** Nouns ending in *-a* that name a man stay masculine: *kolega* (colleague), *turista* (tourist), *dedo* (grandpa), *futbalista*. Slovak puts reality above spelling — just like Italian with *il poeta*.

**Why does this matter now, not later?** Because from unit 4 on, every noun you use will change its ending, and the right ending is decided entirely by this table. The ten seconds you spend writing *(m)*, *(f)*, or *(n)* next to a new word will save you hours of confusion in unit 9.

grammars.title: Bývať and hovoriť — the first two verb classes
body: Slovak verbs fall into three classes according to the vowel in their endings. You've already met two of them in the dialogue; the third comes in unit 7.
after: **How to spot the class: look at the *ja* form.** If it ends in *-ám*, the whole row follows *a*. If it ends in *-ím*, the whole row follows *i*. That's why a good Slovak dictionary always lists the *ja* form next to the dictionary form — and why this course does the same in the list at the back.

**Look at the last row.** The *-ám* class uses *-ajú*, the *-ím* class uses *-ia*. These two are the ones most often wrong at first, because they sound alike and don't follow the pattern of the rows above.

Other verbs in the *-ám* class: *mať* (mám), *volať* (volám), *čakať* (čakám), *poznať* (poznám), *pracovať*… no, that last one is the third class. Verbs in the *-ím* class: *robiť* (robím), *učiť sa* (učím sa), *prosiť* (prosím), *myslieť* (myslím), *sedieť* (sedím).

blocks.text: Three columns that always come up at a first meeting. Notice that all three are built from the same root but are never quite the same — which is exactly why this table exists.

Notice how many country names end in **-sko**: *Slovensko, Poľsko, Nemecko, Anglicko, Maďarsko, Japonsko*. The ending practically means "land" — so *Slovensko* is "the land of the Slováks". When you meet a new country name ending in *-sko*, you can guess the nationality, and vice versa.

blocks.title: Neighbors on every side
items: Slovakia borders **five** countries: Česko, Poľsko, Ukrajina, Maďarsko, and Rakúsko. Bratislava is the only capital in the world that borders two countries at once — Austria and Hungary, both reachable by bike from the city center.
Of those five neighbors, **Czech is practically the same language**. Slovaks and Czechs each speak their own language and understand each other fully, without ever learning the other one.

sections.title: Asking where someone is from and lives

blocks.text: The questions below cover almost every introduction. The first two are about origin, the last ones about where things stand now — and Slovak uses a different preposition for each.

head: Question
Meaning
Answer
rows: How long have you been here?

blocks.text: **Z** for origin, **v** for where you are now. Each forces a different noun form, and each gets its own unit later — *v* in unit 6, *z* in unit 9. For now treat pairs like *z Indonézie* and *v Bratislave* as whole chunks.

One small trap: **odkiaľ** (where from) and **kde** (where) must not be swapped. Answering *Odkiaľ si?* with *Bývam v Bratislave* gives the wrong information — you've named where you live, not where you're from. Slovaks notice the difference, because almost everyone in Bratislava comes from another town.

exercises.prompt: Write the gender: m, f, or n.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: Odkiaľ si? — Som z Indonézie. — Teraz bývam v Bratislave. — Ešte nehovorím dobre. — Aké jazyky vieš? — Neviem po nemecky.
f — m — n — f — f — n — m — f
